tier_reason: Peer-reviewed IFIP Networking 2023 paper (DOI 10.23919/IFIPNetworking57963.2023.10186365). Its Fig. 3 and Fig. 10 heatmaps show LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3004/3882 vs quiche-quiche 2506/2590 Mbit/s, and the values match the means in the artifact's results/baseline/client-timestamps/goracle*/processed.csv. The artifact repo tumi8/quic-10g-paper (configs/configs/baseline.yml, implementations/{lsquic,quiche}/build_*.sh, quic-interop-runner/) and the AMD EPYC 7543 CPU are public, and the flags can be derived from the build scripts. It is not A because no compiler version is stated: GCC comes from Debian build-essential and Rust from an unpinned 'stable' rustup.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Fig. 3 (default builds, 8 GB HTTP/3 download, 10G link): LSQUIC-LSQUIC pair 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche pair 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x, derived from page data). Fig. 10 (UDP receive buffer raised 32x to 6815744 B, both libraries rebuilt for the host CPU): LSQUIC*-LSQUIC* 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche*-quiche* 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x, derived from page data). The heatmap values are per-pair means (checked against the artifact's processed.csv). The mixed pair of an LSQUIC server and a quiche client drops to 1186 Mbit/s (1616 in Fig. 10).
corrections.workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8 GB file over a 10 Gbit/s link between two dedicated bare-metal hosts, using an extended QUIC Interop Runner. All client/server pairs of 6 QUIC libraries were measured with Cubic/Reno congestion control. The paper states 50 repetitions per pair for Fig. 3. The Fig. 10 rerun used 20 repetitions per pair (configs/configs/baseline-optimized.yml).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From the artifact repo tumi8/quic-10g-paper. Fig. 3: LSQUIC commit f3657f1f is built by implementations/lsquic/build_default.sh with `cmake -DBORINGSSL_DIR=../boringssl .` and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so lsquic's CMakeLists.txt defaults to Debug (-O0 -g3). BoringSSL a9670a8b uses a plain `cmake .`. quiche commit 95af1427 is built with `cargo build --release`. Fig. 10: LSQUIC* uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3 -g0) plus patches/march.patch (-march=native, -DLSQUIC_LOWEST_LOG_LEVEL=LSQ_LOG_INFO). quiche* uses RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release. The C compiler is GCC from Debian build-essential and Rust is the unpinned 'stable' rustup toolchain. No versions are recorded.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed at IFIP Networking 2023 (Barcelona; DOI 10.23919/IFIPNetworking57963.2023.10186365, ISBN 978-3-903176-57-7). The code, configs and raw results are public (github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper), but the compiler versions are not stated, so the record is capped at B. The artifact build scripts show that the Fig. 3 LSQUIC binary was a default-Debug (-O0) build competing against release-built quiche, so that comparison understates LSQUIC. The paper's 'compile flags to optimize for the architecture' step (LSQUIC*) is really Debug to Release -O3 plus -march=native. The win holds only for LSQUIC on both ends: an LSQUIC server with a quiche client reaches just 1186 Mbit/s. The same group's 2026 NOMS follow-up (LSQUIC v4.2.0, quiche 0.23.2, Xeon Gold 6421N) shows a smaller lead of 3605 vs 3241 Mbit/s (~1.11x, derived), with MsQuic at 8250 Mbit/s well ahead of both.

notes: All numbers check out against the paper and the published CSVs. The key new fact is that the baseline-figure LSQUIC was an unoptimized Debug build (lsquic's CMake defaults to Debug when no build type is given), which strengthens rather than weakens the claim against release-built quiche. The metadata is verified: MIT, 1876 stars, last commit 2026-09-20, not archived.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NOMS 2026 paper (now published, DOI 10.1109/NOMS69089.2026.11668379). Its Fig. 2 prints LSQUIC-DPDK 10756 vs upstream MsQuic 8250 and MsQuic-DPDK 7983 Mbit/s. The published processed.csv gives the claimed SR-IOV means (11019 / 8118 / 6168). The framework, configs, LSQUIC-DPDK build script (Release) and CPU (Xeon Gold 6421N) are public. It is not A: the compiler version is not stated, and the kernel MsQuic/LSQUIC/quiche baseline binaries are built from a private LRZ GitLab CI (framework/fetch_artifacts.py), so their flags are not published.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Fig. 2 (plain DPDK, same-implementation pairs, mean of 50 x 8 GiB downloads): LSQUIC-DPDK 10756 Mbit/s vs upstream MsQuic v2.4.8 (kernel UDP with GSO+GRO) 8250 Mbit/s (~1.30x, derived from page data). MsQuic-DPDK reaches 7983 Mbit/s (~1.35x, derived), and upstream LSQUIC reaches 3605 Mbit/s (2.98x, printed). With SR-IOV (quic-bypass-paper measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv, Fig. 5): LSQUIC-DPDK 11019 vs MsQuic-DPDK 8118 (~1.36x) and quiche-DPDK 6168 Mbit/s (~1.79x) (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8 GiB file between two bare-metal hosts with 100 Gbit/s Intel E810 NICs, using the extended QUIC Interop Runner (framework/config/bypass-paper/01-implementation-matrix.conf and 06-dpdk-integration.conf). Same-implementation client/server pairs ran 50 repetitions each. Kernel variants used 32x (6815744 B) socket buffers with NIC offloads on. DPDK variants ran on the physical function (ice) or an SR-IOV virtual function (iavf).
corrections.hardware: Both hosts: Intel Xeon Gold 6421N (32 cores), 512 GiB DDR5, Intel E810-CQDA2 100 Gbit/s NIC, Debian 12 with Linux 6.1.0-17, DPDK v24.11 (paper Appendix Table I).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: LSQUIC-DPDK: quic-dpdk-implementations/lsquic-dpdk/build.sh builds BoringSSL 0.20250212.0 and lsquic-dpdk with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3 -g0 via lsquic CMakeLists). It builds DPDK commit 1b3bf112 with meson -Dplatform=generic, using GCC from Debian 12 build-essential (version not stated). MsQuic-DPDK: build.ps1 -Static -Tls openssl -Config Release -UseDpdk with CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS=-Wno-error=stringop-overflow. The kernel baselines (MsQuic v2.4.8, LSQUIC, quiche) are built by a private LRZ GitLab CI, so their flags are unpublished.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed and published: Spaeth et al., 'Kernel Bypass Surgery: A Viable Procedure for Maximizing QUIC Bandwidth?', NOMS 2026, Rome, pp. 1-8, DOI 10.1109/NOMS69089.2026.11668379. The open preprint is on net.in.tum.de, and the dataset is Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18630971. The two msquic-dpdk tables are not inconsistent: 7983 is plain DPDK on the ice PF and 8118 is SR-IOV on the iavf VF, which the paper finds slightly faster. The comparison pits kernel bypass against kernel sockets. LSQUIC-DPDK needs a DPDK-bound NIC port or SR-IOV VF, runs single-threaded with busy polling, and has no GSO/GRO. The authors note that their MsQuic-DPDK datapath enqueues packets one at a time, which handicaps it. Against upstream MsQuic with GSO+GRO, the lead is ~1.30x. GitHub does not mark the repo as a fork, but it is the full LSQUIC tree (based on v4.2.0) with a DPDK datapath.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed and published: NOMS 2026, Rome, pp. 1-8, DOI 10.1109/NOMS69089.2026.11668379. The open preprint is on net.in.tum.de, and the dataset is Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18630971. The earlier 'DOI TODO / unpublished' note is outdated. This is not a GitHub fork of quiche. It is a small standalone C client/server (about 50 KB of C) that replaces quiche's mio-based example apps with a DPDK busy-polling loop and links the unmodified upstream quiche library through its FFI. The paper states that no quiche library code changed. The comparison pits kernel bypass (a DPDK-bound NIC port or SR-IOV VF, one polling thread) against kernel UDP sockets. quiche-DPDK is the slowest of the four DPDK stacks (LSQUIC-DPDK reaches 10756 Mbit/s) and is below upstream MsQuic with GSO+GRO (8250 Mbit/s). There is no LICENSE file.

notes: The numbers are confirmed and printed directly in paper Fig. 2, so they are not only derived from the CSV. The paper is now published, and the hardware is filled in from Table I. I set is_fork_of to null because GitHub reports fork=false and the repo is a wrapper app around unmodified quiche. The license is still none, so usability stays 'reference', and last_commit 2026-02-12 is verified.
